tr.td: Bentiu and Rubkona, Unity State, South Sudan
The Kalibalek mosque, the Bentiu Civil Hospital and the streets of the Kalibalek market area
Fighters of the SPLA in Opposition, according to the UN human rights investigators and Human Rights Watch; the opposition denies it

Civil war between forces loyal to President Salva Kiir and to his sacked deputy Riek Machar, begun in December 2013

content.p: When rebel forces took the town of Bentiu in South Sudan's oil-producing Unity State on 15 April 2014, hundreds of civilians who had gone to a mosque, a hospital and other places of shelter were shot dead. The United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS) later concluded that there were reasonable grounds to believe that fighters affiliated with the opposition SPLA/IO carried out the attacks at the mosque and the hospital, and that victims were singled out by ethnicity, nationality and perceived loyalty to the government. The opposition has denied it. Nobody is reported to have been tried.

The killings came as the civil war that began in December 2013 had, in the words of an Al Jazeera correspondent in Bentiu, taken on an ethnic dimension. Human Rights Watch said they triggered an attack two days later on a UN base in Bor.
content.h2: A town that had changed hands four times
content.p: Bentiu, the capital of Unity State, faces its twin town Rubkona across the Bahr el Ghazal river. According to Human Rights Watch, Bentiu was largely Nuer in population and had changed hands four times since the war began. The general commanding the army's Division 4 at Rubkona, James Koang, announced his defection to the opposition on 21 December 2013. Government troops, fighting alongside fighters of the Sudanese rebel Justice and Equality Movement (JEM), retook the town on 10 January 2014, and spent the following weeks burning and looting villages to the south and east, Human Rights Watch reported.

Radio Tamazuj, a news outlet covering the region, described the two sides this way. The government army was loyal to Kiir, a Dinka, and recruited from several communities. The rebel force was loyal to the ousted vice president Riek Machar, a Nuer, and was drawn mostly from defected soldiers and allied civilian militia. JEM, whose fighters were largely Darfuri, Arab or Nuba, had earlier used Unity State as a rear base, and had fought on the government's side. According to Machar's rebels, as reported by Radio Tamazuj, JEM's involvement was purely mercenary. On 15 April, the UN account says, fighters at the hospital were looking for JEM members, among others, and accused the Sudanese men they gathered of supporting the SPLA.
By mid-April, the town had refilled. The people who had fled in December and January returned in numbers, among them foreign traders, civil servants, labourers and police, according to Radio Tamazuj.

The UN investigators' account, excerpted by Radio Tamazuj, describes rumours of an imminent opposition assault and a campaign to keep civilians away from the UN base. Reportedly the army manning a checkpoint near the base was told by a senior state official to let no civilians pass. On 14 April, at least two witnesses saw a high-ranking state official instruct soldiers at the Bentiu bridge to stop anyone from crossing. A state government member reportedly told traders in the Kalibalek area that they were being protected, yet many traders tried to reach the UN camp anyway and were turned back. Human Rights Watch said that the governor reassured people that the situation was under control.

The traders instead sheltered in the Kalibalek mosque. According to the UN account, police or army officers reportedly requisitioned traders' trucks to move troops, and those who refused were allegedly beaten. A committee of seven traders asked the police for protection and, after the station head asked for 100 South Sudanese pounds per officer, about a dozen police were sent to guard the mosque. They fled when the opposition reached the town centre between 9 and 10 a.m. on 15 April.

The UN account describes three groups of armed men entering the mosque compound in turn. The first, about 20 fighters in a mixture of uniforms and civilian clothes, shot several people in the courtyard, then robbed those near the doors and windows before leaving without killing more. The second group demanded money and phones, and then, in a sequence the investigators say remains unclear, fighters opened fire. One man in military uniform with a machine gun appeared to shoot from a doorway, while others fired through the windows.

UN human rights officers who visited on 21 and 24 April found all 12 windows broken and more than 185 spent cartridge cases inside and outside the building. An analysis by an independent international organisation in May found a mix of rifle and machine-gun cartridges, with the machine-gun cases concentrated at one door and the adjacent veranda.

After the shooting, the fighters called on people to identify their nationality or community. According to the account, an Ethiopian trader was recognised and helped out, and when Ethiopians were called to identify themselves, six people who identified as Ethiopian, two of them in fact Darfuris, were escorted to the hospital. A group who came forward as Misseriya was taken to the minaret, where a Nuer fighter argued that Darfuris must be among them, and others opened fire. Witnesses put the dead in that shooting at 15, 30 or 40. A Darfuri survivor told Human Rights Watch that the shooting inside the mosque began around 1:30 p.m. and that people next to him cried out as they were hit.

Later in the afternoon two SPLA/IO officers arrived. One source told the UN that the officers expressed dissatisfaction with the killings, and that one of them allegedly stopped a fighter who was firing on civilians in the yard. They said they would keep providing security only if their bodyguards were paid: the traders offered 1,500 pounds, the officers asked 5,000, and other sources named sums between 3,000 and 8,000. The traders collected the money.

That night survivors were taken to the hospital, and about 30 able-bodied people were chosen to load bodies on to a dump truck. According to credible witnesses, over 250 bodies went on the truck and at least 37 were left behind. Nine survivors were forced to ride on top of the bodies on a journey of more than two hours that took them past Khaljak, 30 kilometres from Bentiu, and a few kilometres further along a side track. According to one source, an SPLA/IO officer told them to tip the bodies into a drainage trench. They were later dropped at a checkpoint and told to walk to the UN camp. UN officers saw the 37 remaining bodies removed from the mosque on 20, 23 and 25 April.

People had begun gathering at the Bentiu Civil Hospital on 14 April, Nuer and Dinka civilians along with Sudanese and Ethiopian nationals. By about 8:30 or 9 a.m. on 15 April, witnesses told the UN, armed fighters had arrived, and shot two to four Darfuris at the main gate. Between 20 and 50 entered the compound and searched it room by room, asking for government officials, Dinka and JEM members. Some Nuer who had been hiding came out to greet them and cheer. In the staff accommodation building, fighters shot through a locked door, killing at least four people inside, all Nuer according to the report. Fighters also gathered about 80 men, largely Darfuri and Nuban, near the cemetery and picked out some by name, among them a Dinka state government official who was shot in the back, according to two witnesses.

The UN report counts at least 19 civilians killed at the hospital. A doctor at the scene told Human Rights Watch that at least 18 died. Human Rights Watch noted in a footnote that the UN had estimated 20 and that Medecins Sans Frontieres had reported 21 Darfuris and five Nuer killed.

Elsewhere in the Kalibalek area, one witness described soldiers executing five Sudanese men on the approach road to the mosque. UN officers counted 81 bodies in that area over 20 to 24 April, 79 in civilian clothing, at 21 locations. In at least four of them the dead had hands tied behind their backs or bullet holes in the head. A Nuer civil servant told Human Rights Watch that he walked the town beside rebel soldiers and watched them kill people in the market.

Some opposition fighters acted to stop the killing. Radio Tamazuj noted that in at least one mass killing a group of rebels was halted midway by another group, and Human Rights Watch heard from one witness that Koang sent soldiers to stop violence at the hospital later on 15 April.

The figures differ by source. The first UNMISS statement, on 21 April, said more than 200 civilians were reportedly killed and more than 400 wounded at the mosque, and that it had reports of comparable attacks at a Catholic church, at a World Food Programme compound that had been emptied, and at the hospital. The African Union Commission's chairperson repeated that figure the next day. Human Rights Watch wrote in its August 2014 report of at least 200 killed in a mosque and a hospital. The UN's detailed report put the dead at about 287 at the mosque and at least 19 at the hospital, and added that bodies found elsewhere suggested more. Sudanese community leaders gave UN officers 333 names of people they believed killed in Bentiu and Rubkona on 15 April, 273 of them at the mosque, ranging in age from two to over 70. The UN said that was roughly consistent with its own interviews.
content.h2: Who did it, and what they said
content.p: Radio Tamazuj reported in May 2014 that survivors named rebels as the perpetrators and that no individual perpetrator had been identified. It listed as plausible motives ethnic hatred, revenge for abuses by government forces and their JEM allies earlier in the year, and greed, since many accounts mention robbery before shooting. The outlet noted that the foreign minister and an army spokesman had said Arab militia or mercenaries called Janjaweed were involved, but found no credible independent witness account of it.

The UN report concluded that both the hospital and mosque attacks came after the opposition controlled the town, that survivors described most attackers as uniformed and carrying military weapons, and that senior officers arrived only after fighting ended. It also said that UN human rights officers were told by opposition officials on 21 and 25 April that opposition forces had nothing to do with the killings. One implied that the mosque dead were JEM fighters, and might have been killed by armed Nuer civilians in revenge. The report said no evidence was offered. The opposition's spokesman, Lul Ruai Koang, said retreating government forces committed the killings.

Machar told Al Jazeera on 22 April that he had contacted the commander in Bentiu, who told him the accusation was false, and that his forces would not kill their own people. South Sudan's foreign minister answered that they were Machar's rebels and that he had to answer for what they did. Machar later acknowledged the killings in an interview on the BBC programme Hard Talk and said he would investigate. General Koang told Human Rights Watch that deaths at the hospital had occurred, but that those in the mosque had been exaggerated and were JEM fighters, though he admitted they had no weapons.

The UN also accused the opposition of using Radio Bentiu to broadcast hate speech inciting killing and rape. Toby Lanzer, the UN's representative, said that people associated with the opposition had used an FM station for that purpose.

The UN base's numbers rose from about 12,000 on 15 April to 22,500 by 22 April, according to the UN report. Human Rights Watch reported more than 25,000, with 10,000 arriving in a single day. UNMISS carried more than 150 Darfuris from the hospital to the base on 16 April and later handed over more than 100 of them to JEM commanders, who took them out of Bentiu, Human Rights Watch said.

The attack was followed on 17 April by an assault on the UN base in Bor, where about 50 people were killed, most of the camp's residents being Nuer. Human Rights Watch said the Bor attack was triggered by the opposition's capture of Bentiu, and that the government spokesman said Nuer in the camp had provoked it by celebrating that capture.

The White House said it was horrified by reports that fighters aligned with Machar had massacred hundreds, calling the violence an abomination. On 22 April the AU Commission's chairperson condemned the "deliberate and criminal attack on civilians" and urged both sides to cooperate with a regional monitoring mechanism so that perpetrators could be brought to justice. Within days President Kiir removed army chief James Hoth Mai, giving no reason, and the intelligence chief. SBS reported that sources linked the army move to military setbacks in the north, and that the US and France asked the UN Security Council to consider sanctions. Human Rights Watch urged the Council to order a fact-finding mission and to impose sanctions on individuals in both government and opposition forces.

The African Union's Commission of Inquiry, according to its final report, made a mission to South Sudan from 26 May to 4 June that included Bentiu, and another from 31 July to 3 August to Bentiu, Rubkona and Leer County. Human Rights Watch, writing in August, said that as far as it could ascertain the opposition had made no effort to hold its forces to account for the killings in Bentiu and other crimes. The pages consulted report no prosecutions.
